The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$S:D(S)\subseteq H\to H$ be a densely defined closable antilinear operator.
Its graph closure $\overline S$ is closed and has the polar decomposition
$$\overline S=J|\overline S|,\qquad |\overline S|=(\overline S^{\,*}\overline S)^{1/2}.$$
Here $J$ is antilinear, vanishes on $\ker\overline S$, and is isometric on
$(\ker\overline S)^\perp$; if $\overline S$ is injective and has dense range,
$J$ is antiunitary.

For a concrete von Neumann algebra $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ and a vector
$\Omega$ cyclic and separating for $M$, define
$D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Then $S_0$ is
well defined, densely defined, antilinear, and closable.

argument. If $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, its **conjugate Hilbert space**
$\overline H$ consists of symbols $\overline x$ for $x\in H$, with
$\overline x+\overline y=\overline{x+y}$,
$a\,\overline x=\overline{\overline a\,x}$ for $a\in\mathbb C$, and
$$\langle\overline x,\overline y\rangle_{\overline H} :=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle_H}.$$
The canonical map $c_H:H\to\overline H$, $c_Hx=\overline x$, is a
conjugate-linear surjective isometry.

Hilbert norm. It is densely defined when $D(A)$ is dense in $H_1$, and closed
when $\Gamma(A)$ is closed.

For a densely defined linear operator $A:D(A)\subseteq H_1\to H_2$, define

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in its first argument. An operator $\rho\in\mathcal B(H)$ is a **density operator** when it is positive, trace class, and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Here trace class means compact with summable singular values, and $\operatorname{Tr}$ is the basis-independent trace of a trace-class operator.

The **normal density state represented by $\rho$** is the functional on bounded operators
$
\omega_\rho(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),\qquad A\in\mathcal B(H).
$
In this page, “normal density state” means this specified trace-pairing representation; no equivalence with other definitions of normal functionals is assumed. The trace pairing is used only for bounded $A$. Unbounded observables are treated through their spectral probability measures in [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital $*$-subalgebra closed in the weak operator topology. Then $M''=M$, and $M$ is also closed in the strong operator topology. Consequently the concrete von Neumann algebras of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]] are exactly the unital $*$-subalgebras that are closed in either of these topologies. For an arbitrary set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ one has $W^*(\mathcal S)''=W^*(\mathcal S)$.

Here a complex C$^*$-algebra is a complex Banach algebra with associative bilinear multiplication, submultiplicative norm, and a conjugate-linear involution satisfying $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$; **unital** means that it has a nonzero identity $I$ ([[def-c-star-algebra]]). A $*$-automorphism is a bijective complex-linear map preserving multiplication and involution. Let $t\mapsto\alpha_t$ be a strongly continuous one-parameter group of such automorphisms, so $\alpha_0$ is the identity and $\alpha_s\alpha_t=\alpha_{s+t}$. It is **strongly continuous** when $t\mapsto\alpha_t(A)$ is norm-continuous for each fixed $A\in\mathcal A$. A **state** is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(A^*A)\ge0$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$; this is the state convention of [[def-qsm-infinite-algebraic-state]].

$$S_b:=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\le\operatorname{Im}z\le b\},\qquad S_b^\circ:=\{z\in\mathbb C:0<\operatorname{Im}z<b\}.$$

A state $\omega$ is a **$\beta$-KMS state for $\alpha$ in physical time** when for every $A,B\in\mathcal A$ there is a bounded function $F_{A,B}:S_b\to\mathbb C$ (that is, $\sup_{z\in S_b}|F_{A,B}(z)|<\infty$) that is continuous on $S_b$, complex-differentiable at every point of $S_b^\circ$, and satisfies

$$F_{A,B}(t)=\omega\!\left(A\alpha_t(B)\right),\qquad F_{A,B}(t+ib)=\omega\!\left(\alpha_t(B)A\right)\quad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

For the assigned quantum spin model, $\mathcal A$ is the norm-completed quasi-local algebra of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]] and $\alpha$ is the thermodynamic dynamics of [[thm-qsm-finite-range-spin-dynamics]], under that theorem's stated hypotheses. The strip width is $\beta\hbar$ in physical seconds; setting $\hbar=1$ is a separate natural-unit convention. This is a mathematical equilibrium criterion for the specified algebra and dynamics. It does not assert that a model describes a material, that a system has dynamically relaxed, or that all stationary states are KMS.

derivations.claim: Let $M=\{L_A:A\in M_n(\mathbb C)\}$ on $\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$, where $L_A X=AX$. The Hilbert-Schmidt adjoint satisfies $L_A^*=L_{A^*}$, so $M$ is a unital star subalgebra. The ambient operator space $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_{\rm HS})$ is finite dimensional; hence $M$ is weak-operator closed. By [F2], $M$ is a concrete von Neumann algebra. Since $\rho^{1/2}$ is invertible, every $X\in\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$ equals $L_{X\rho^{-1/2}}\Omega$, so $\Omega$ is cyclic. If $L_A\Omega=0$, then $A\rho^{1/2}=0$ and invertibility gives $A=0$, so $\Omega$ is separating. Finally, $$\langle L_A\Omega,\Omega\rangle_{\rm HS}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^{1/2}A\rho^{1/2})=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),$$ using finite trace cyclicity.

For $A,B\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ define $$F_{A,B}(z)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\rho A e^{izH/\hbar}Be^{-izH/\hbar}\right).$$ Finite matrix exponentials are entire, so $F_{A,B}$ is entire. If $0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq\beta\hbar$, the real-time factors are unitary and the two imaginary-time factors have norms at most $e^{\beta\|H\|}$ each. Since $\|\rho\|_1=1$, $|F_{A,B}(z)|\leq\|A\|\|B\|e^{2\beta\|H\|}$ uniformly on that strip. The group $\alpha_s$ is norm-continuous because its matrix entries are continuous.

Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\rho$, with eigenvalues $p_j>0$, and write $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$. Then $E_{ij}\Omega=\sqrt{p_j}E_{ij}$ and $E_{ij}^*\Omega=\sqrt{p_i}E_{ji}$, whence $S(E_{ij})=\sqrt{p_i/p_j}\,E_{ji}$. The maps $JX=X^*$ and $\Delta X=\rho X\rho^{-1}$ satisfy $J\Delta^{1/2}E_{ij}=\sqrt{p_i/p_j}\,E_{ji}$ and $\Delta E_{ij}=(p_i/p_j)E_{ij}$. For $X\in\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$, $$\Delta^{it}L_A\Delta^{-it}X=\rho^{it}A\rho^{-it}X,$$ because $\Delta^{-it}X=\rho^{-it}X\rho^{it}$ and the final right factor $\rho^{it}$ cancels $\rho^{-it}$. Hence $\sigma_t(A)=\rho^{it}A\rho^{-it}$.

For $\rho=e^{-\beta H}/Z$, functional calculus gives $\rho^{it}=Z^{-it}e^{-i\beta tH}$; the scalar factor cancels in conjugation. Substituting $t=-s/(\beta\hbar)$ into step 3.1 yields $\sigma_{-s/(\beta\hbar)}(A)=e^{isH/\hbar}Ae^{-isH/\hbar}=\alpha_s(A)$. Here $\beta\hbar$ has units seconds, so the modular parameter is dimensionless.

At $z=t+i\beta\hbar$, write $U=e^{itH/\hbar}$. Since $U$ commutes with $e^{\pm\beta H}$, $$F_{A,B}(t+i\beta\hbar)=Z^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(e^{-\beta H}A e^{-\beta H}\alpha_t(B)e^{\beta H}\right) =Z^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(Ae^{-\beta H}\alpha_t(B)\right) =\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\rho\alpha_t(B)A\right).$$ The middle equality cycles $e^{\beta H}$ past the trace, and the last cycles $A$ past the trace. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a set and let
$\mathcal{F}_0$ be a filter on $X$ ([[def-filter]]). Then there is an ultrafilter
$\mathcal{U}$ on $X$ ([[def-ultrafilter]]) with $\mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{U}$.

The hypothesis is spent exactly once, through Zorn's lemma at step 4.1; the rest
of the argument is a theorem of ZF.

In particular, every set that carries a filter carries an ultrafilter. The proof
uses Zorn's lemma ([[thm-zorn]]) and therefore the Axiom of Choice. That some
choice principle is unavoidable here, if ZF is consistent, is an external
independence result, not proved in this library; see the remarks below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and write its polar decomposition as $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. The preceding Tomita-operator lemma ensures this closure and polar data are well defined, with $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective. For $x\in\mathcal B(H)$ and dimensionless $t\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sigma_t(x):=\Delta^{it}x\Delta^{-it}.$$
Set $\omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$. The powers $\Delta^{it}$ are the bounded unitary imaginary powers from the unbounded Borel functional calculus. At this definition stage $\sigma_t$ is defined on $\mathcal B(H)$; preservation of $M$ is established by a separate theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector that is cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ on $M\Omega$ and $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and $F=S^*$. Then $S$ is a densely defined closed antilinear involution, its polar decomposition is $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ with $J$ antiunitary and $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective, and
$$J=J^*=J^{-1},\qquad J\Delta J=\Delta^{-1},\qquad J\Delta^{it}J=\Delta^{it}\ (t\in\mathbb R),\qquad F=J\Delta^{-1/2}=\Delta^{1/2}J,\qquad J\Omega=\Omega,\qquad \Delta\Omega=\Omega.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von
Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space $H$, and define
$$M_\perp:=\{T\in\mathcal S_1(H):\operatorname{Tr}(Tx)=0 \text{ for every }x\in M\}.$$
Equip the coset space $Q:=\mathcal S_1(H)/M_\perp$ with the quotient norm.
Then the trace pairing
$$\Psi:M\to Q^*,\qquad (\Psi(x))([T])=\operatorname{Tr}(Tx),$$
is a well-defined isometric bijection, and $Q$ is a Banach space. Thus $Q$ is
an isometric predual of $M$, and its dual unit ball is weak-star compact.
Every vector functional $x\mapsto\langle x\xi,\xi\rangle$ and every positive
functional in $Q$ preserves suprema of bounded increasing positive nets in
$M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, and let
$\mathcal S_1(H)$ be its trace-class operators with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
and trace $\operatorname{Tr}$. Finite-rank operators are dense in
$(\mathcal S_1(H),\|\cdot\|_1)$. For every bounded linear functional
$\Phi:\mathcal S_1(H)\to\mathbb C$, there is a unique $X\in\mathcal B(H)$ such
that
$$\Phi(T)=\operatorname{Tr}(TX)\qquad(T\in\mathcal S_1(H)),$$
and the correspondence is isometric:
$\|\Phi\|=\|X\|$.

**Assume the ultrafilter lemma.**  If $X$ is a real or complex normed space,
then its closed dual unit ball $B_{X^*}$ is compact in the weak-star topology
$\sigma(X^*,X)$.  Completeness of $X$ is not required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

Assume AC. For a bounded self-adjoint operator $T$ on a nonzero complex Hilbert space there is a unique isometric unital star-homomorphism $C(\sigma(T))\to\mathcal B(H)$, $f\mapsto f(T)$, sending the coordinate function $z$ to $T$, with range $C^*(I,T)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $f$ be meromorphic on $\Omega$ with
pole set $S$, and let $\Gamma$ be admissible for the residue theorem in
$\Omega$. Then

$\int_\Gamma f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_{a\in S}n(\Gamma,a)\operatorname{Res}(f,a),$

where only finitely many terms are nonzero.

Assume countable choice. If $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f\in L^1$, then
$$g(x)=\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi$$
is bounded and continuous, equals f almost everywhere, and equals the specified value at every Lebesgue point of f.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be a positive self-adjoint injective operator with spectral projection valued measure $E$ supported on $(0,\infty)$. For $t\in\mathbb R$, the unbounded Borel functional calculus defines $A^{it}$ as a unitary on all of $H$. For every $\xi\in H$, the map $t\mapsto A^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $|\lambda|=1$ with $\lambda\ne-1$. Write $\lambda=e^{i\theta}$ with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$, set $\alpha=(1+\lambda)^{-1}$, and note $\alpha+\bar\alpha=1$. Because $\Delta$ is positive, its spectrum lies in $[0,\infty)$; $-\lambda\notin[0,\infty)$, so $(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}$ is a bounded spectral multiplier.

First let $x'\in M'$ be a positive contraction. In the linear-second notation $(u|v)=\langle v,u\rangle$, define $\psi(y)=(x'\Omega|y\Omega)=\omega(x'y)$ and $\psi_x(y)=\omega(\alpha xy+\bar\alpha yx)$ for $y\in M$ and $x=x^*\in M$. Since $x'$ commutes with $M$, $0\leq\psi\leq\omega$, and $\psi$ is normal by its rank-one trace-class representation. Each $\psi_x$ is self-adjoint. For fixed $y$, both $x\mapsto\omega(xy)$ and $x\mapsto\omega(yx)$ are normal matrix-coefficient functionals, so $x\mapsto\psi_x$ is continuous from the weak-star topology of $M_{\rm sa}$ to the pointwise topology of $M_*^{\rm sa}$. The self-adjoint unit ball of $M$ is weak-star closed; [F3]–[F4] make it compact. Hence $V=\{\psi_x:x=x^*,\ \|x\|\leq1\}$ is compact and convex.

Suppose $\psi\notin V$. The pointwise topology on $M_*^{\rm sa}$ has a base of finite evaluation conditions, so there are self-adjoint $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in M$ for which $q=(\psi(a_j))_{j=1}^m$ is outside the compact convex set $K=\{(\phi(a_j))_{j=1}^m:\phi\in V\}\subset\mathbb R^m$. Choose $0<r<\operatorname{dist}(q,K)$, put $U=K+B(0,r)$, choose $u_0\in U$, and set $C=U-u_0$. The open convex neighborhood $C$ of $0$ is absorbing; its gauge $p(v)=\inf\{s>0:v\in sC\}$ is finite and sublinear, and convexity and openness give $C=\{v:p(v)<1\}$. With $v_0=q-u_0\notin C$, $p(v_0)\geq1$. On the line $\mathbb Rv_0$ define $f(tv_0)=t\,p(v_0)$. Positive homogeneity gives $f\leq p$ for $t\geq0$; for $t<0$ the inequality $p(v_0)+p(-v_0)\geq0$ gives the same domination. By [F5], extend $f$ to a real linear $L$ on $\mathbb R^m$ with $L\leq p$. Then $L(k-u_0)<1\leq L(q-u_0)$ for every $k\in K$. Writing $L(z)=\sum_j c_jz_j$ and $y_0=\sum_jc_ja_j\in M_{\rm sa}$ gives $\psi(y_0)>\sup_{\|x\|\leq1,\ x=x^*}\psi_x(y_0)$.

Fix $|\lambda|=1$, $\lambda=e^{i\theta}$, $-\pi<\theta<\pi$. For $n\geq1$ let $E_n=1_{[1/n,n]}(\Delta)$. On $E_nH$, $\Delta$ and its inverse are bounded. Apply [F8] to each scalar matrix coefficient of $$f_n(z)=\frac{e^{i\theta z}}{\sin(\pi z)}\Delta^{-z}E_nxE_n\Delta^z$$ around the rectangle $-1/2\leq\operatorname{Re}z\leq1/2$, $|\operatorname{Im}z|\leq R$. On $E_nH$, $\log\Delta$ is bounded, so $f_n$ is norm-meromorphic with simple poles at integers; the rectangle encloses only $0$, with residue $E_nxE_n/\pi$. On the horizontal sides, the norm is at most $2e^{|\theta|R}n^2\|x\|/(e^{\pi R}-e^{-\pi R})$, which tends to zero. On the right vertical side, $z=it+1/2$ gives $\sin(\pi z)=\cosh(\pi t)$, $e^{i\theta z}=e^{-\theta t}e^{i\theta/2}$, and $\Delta^{-z}E_nxE_n\Delta^z=\Delta^{-1/2}\Delta^{-it}E_nxE_n\Delta^{it}\Delta^{1/2}$. On the left side, $z=it-1/2$ gives $\sin(\pi z)=-\cosh(\pi t)$ and the corresponding factors $\Delta^{1/2}\Delta^{-it}E_nxE_n\Delta^{it}\Delta^{-1/2}$ and $e^{-\theta t}e^{-i\theta/2}$. Substitution in the oriented contour formula therefore gives $$E_nxE_n=\Delta^{1/2}E_n\widetilde xE_n\Delta^{-1/2}+\lambda\Delta^{-1/2}E_n\widetilde xE_n\Delta^{1/2},\qquad \widetilde x=e^{-i\theta/2}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-\theta t}}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}\Delta^{-it}x\Delta^{it}\,dt.$$ The scalar weight is integrable because $|\theta|<\pi$. For fixed $\xi\in H$, the orbit $t\mapsto\Delta^{-it}x\Delta^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous: writing $U_t=\Delta^{-it}$, $\|U_txU_t^*\xi-U_sxU_s^*\xi\|\leq\|x\|\|(U_t^*-U_s^*)\xi\|+\|(U_t-U_s)xU_s^*\xi\|,$ and each term tends to zero as $t\to s$ by [F10]. Its norm is at most $\|x\|\|\xi\|$. Define the integral as the norm limit of ordinary vector integrals over finite intervals; the integrable scalar weight makes the tails Cauchy. The resulting linear map has norm at most $\|x\|$ times the weight's $L^1$ norm, so it is a bounded operator. This contour identity has the normalization fixed by the residue $E_nxE_n/\pi$.

The last strict inequality is impossible. Positivity and $0\leq\psi\leq\omega$ imply $\psi(y_0)\leq\psi(|y_0|)\leq\omega(|y_0|)$. For $n\geq1$, let $x_n=f_n(y_0)$ by [F6], where $f_n(s)=s/(|s|+1/n)$. Each $x_n$ is self-adjoint with $\|x_n\|\leq1$ and commutes with $y_0$. The positive functions $g_n(s)=s^2/(|s|+1/n)$ increase to $|s|$, so $x_ny_0=y_0x_n=g_n(y_0)\uparrow|y_0|$. Normality gives $\psi_{x_n}(y_0)=\omega(g_n(y_0))\uparrow\omega(|y_0|)$, contradicting the strict separator. Therefore $\psi=\psi_x$ for some self-adjoint contraction $x$.

Apply the same residue calculation to $g_n(z)=e^{i\theta z}\Delta^{-z}E_n/\sin(\pi z)$, whose residue at $0$ is $E_n/\pi$. On the right vertical side its multiplier is $2e^{-\theta t}e^{i\theta/2}\Delta^{-1/2}\Delta^{-it}E_n/(e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t})$; on the left it is $-2e^{-\theta t}e^{-i\theta/2}\Delta^{1/2}\Delta^{-it}E_n/(e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t})$. Including the opposite orientations of the two vertical sides and using $\lambda=e^{i\theta}$ yields $$\Delta^{1/2}(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}E_n=e^{-i\theta/2}\left(\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-\theta t}}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}\Delta^{-it}\,dt\right)E_n.$$ This follows by factoring $\Delta^{-1/2}(\Delta+\lambda)=\Delta^{1/2}+\lambda\Delta^{-1/2}$ from the vertical-side integral. Define the strong integral vectorwise as in step 1.4. The bounded spectral multiplier on the left and the integrable weight on the right allow $n\to\infty$ strongly, so the identity holds with $E_n$ omitted. In particular the scalar factor has no additional $i$: at $\lambda=1$ and $\Delta=I$ both sides equal $1/2$.

For every $y\in M$, $\psi=\psi_x$ and $\alpha+\bar\alpha=1$ give $$(x'\Omega-\bar\alpha x\Omega|y\Omega)=\omega(x'y)-\alpha\omega(xy)=\bar\alpha\,\omega(yx)=(S_0y\Omega|\bar\alpha x\Omega).$$ The antilinear-adjoint definition therefore puts $\bar\alpha x\Omega$ in $D(F)$ and gives $F(\bar\alpha x\Omega)=x'\Omega-\bar\alpha x\Omega$, or $\alpha F(x\Omega)=x'\Omega-\bar\alpha x\Omega$. Since $x=x^*$, $Sx\Omega=x\Omega$; hence $x\Omega\in D(\Delta)$ and $F(x\Omega)=\Delta x\Omega$. Thus $x'\Omega=(\alpha\Delta+\bar\alpha)x\Omega=(\Delta+\lambda)x\Omega/(1+\lambda)$. Replacing $x$ by $x/(1+\lambda)$ proves $(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}x'\Omega\in M\Omega$. For a general $x'\in M'$, write $x'=h_1+ih_2$ with $h_j=h_j^*$. If $c\geq\max(1,\|h_1\|,\|h_2\|)$, each $(I\pm h_j/c)/2$ is a positive contraction, so $x'$ is a complex linear combination of positive contractions. Linearity extends the inclusion to all of $M'\Omega$. Uniqueness follows because $\Delta+\lambda$ is injective and $\Omega$ is separating.

Let $x'\in M'$ and $x\in M$ satisfy $x'\Omega=(\Delta+\lambda)x\Omega$. For $y_1,y_2\in M$, commutation, $\Delta=FS$, $S(y\Omega)=y^*\Omega$, and $S=J\Delta^{1/2}=\Delta^{-1/2}J$ give $$(y_1\Omega|x'y_2\Omega)=(y_2^*y_1\Omega|x'\Omega)=(Sx\Omega|S(y_2^*y_1\Omega))+\lambda(y_1\Omega|y_2x\Omega)=(y_1x^*\Omega|y_2\Omega)+\lambda(y_1\Omega|S(x^*S(y_2\Omega)))=(\Delta^{-1/2}JxJ\Delta^{1/2}y_1\Omega|y_2\Omega)+\lambda(y_1\Omega|\Delta^{-1/2}Jx^*J\Delta^{1/2}y_2\Omega).$$ If $y_1\Omega,y_2\Omega\in(\Delta+1)^{-1}M'\Omega$, then both lie in $D(\Delta^{1/2})\cap D(\Delta^{-1/2})$. Since $JxJ$ is bounded with adjoint $Jx^*J$, $$(\Delta^{-1/2}JxJ\Delta^{1/2}y_1\Omega|y_2\Omega)=(JxJ\Delta^{1/2}y_1\Omega|\Delta^{-1/2}y_2\Omega)=(\Delta^{1/2}y_1\Omega|Jx^*J\Delta^{-1/2}y_2\Omega),$$ and self-adjointness of $\Delta^{-1/2}$ gives $$(y_1\Omega|\Delta^{-1/2}Jx^*J\Delta^{1/2}y_2\Omega)=(\Delta^{-1/2}y_1\Omega|Jx^*J\Delta^{1/2}y_2\Omega).$$ Therefore $$(y_1\Omega|x'y_2\Omega)=(\Delta^{1/2}y_1\Omega|Jx^*J\Delta^{-1/2}y_2\Omega)+\lambda(\Delta^{-1/2}y_1\Omega|Jx^*J\Delta^{1/2}y_2\Omega).$$

The space $\Delta^{-1/2}M'\Omega$ is dense: $F(y'\Omega)=y'^*\Omega$ and $F=J\Delta^{-1/2}$ give $\Delta^{-1/2}M'\Omega=JM'\Omega$, which is dense by cyclicity of $\Omega$ for $M'$. In particular each $y'\Omega$ belongs to $D(\Delta^{-1/2})$. Fix $\xi\in D(\Delta^{1/2})\cap D(\Delta^{-1/2})$ and put $\eta=(\Delta^{1/2}+\Delta^{-1/2})\xi\in H$. Choose $y_n'\in M'$ so that $\eta_n:=\Delta^{-1/2}y_n'\Omega\to\eta$ in $H$. Step 3.1 at $\lambda=1$ supplies $y_n\in M$ with $y_n\Omega=(\Delta+1)^{-1}y_n'\Omega$. The spectral calculus gives $$y_n\Omega=q(\Delta)\eta_n,\qquad \Delta^{1/2}y_n\Omega=a(\Delta)\eta_n,\qquad \Delta^{-1/2}y_n\Omega=b(\Delta)\eta_n,$$ where $q(\lambda)=\sqrt\lambda/(1+\lambda)$, $a(\lambda)=\lambda/(1+\lambda)$ and $b(\lambda)=1/(1+\lambda)$ for $\lambda>0$. These three multipliers are bounded. The identities follow by multiplying their scalar functions on the domain of $\Delta^{-1/2}$; moreover $\lambda^{1/2}q(\lambda)=a(\lambda)$ and $\lambda^{-1/2}q(\lambda)=b(\lambda)$ are bounded, so $q(\Delta)\eta_n$ belongs to both required domains. Applied to $\eta$, the same identities give $q(\Delta)\eta=\xi$, $a(\Delta)\eta=\Delta^{1/2}\xi$ and $b(\Delta)\eta=\Delta^{-1/2}\xi$. Thus convergence of $\eta_n$ in $H$ implies $y_n\Omega\to\xi$ and $\Delta^{\pm1/2}y_n\Omega\to\Delta^{\pm1/2}\xi$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and write its polar decomposition as $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. The preceding Tomita-operator lemma ensures this closure and polar data are well defined, with $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective. For $x\in\mathcal B(H)$ and dimensionless $t\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sigma_t(x):=\Delta^{it}x\Delta^{-it}.$$
Set $\omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$. The powers $\Delta^{it}$ are the bounded unitary imaginary powers from the unbounded Borel functional calculus. At this definition stage $\sigma_t$ is defined on $\mathcal B(H)$; preservation of $M$ is established by a separate theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector that is cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ on $M\Omega$ and $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and $F=S^*$. Then $S$ is a densely defined closed antilinear involution, its polar decomposition is $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ with $J$ antiunitary and $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective, and
$$J=J^*=J^{-1},\qquad J\Delta J=\Delta^{-1},\qquad J\Delta^{it}J=\Delta^{it}\ (t\in\mathbb R),\qquad F=J\Delta^{-1/2}=\Delta^{1/2}J,\qquad J\Omega=\Omega,\qquad \Delta\Omega=\Omega.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standard modular data of a concrete von Neumann algebra $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ with unit cyclic-separating vector $\Omega$. Let $F=S^*$, where $S$ is the closure of $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$, and let $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $|\lambda|=1$ and $\lambda\ne-1$,
$$(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}M'\Omega\subseteq M\Omega.$$
The modular conjugation and operator satisfy
$$JMJ=M',\qquad \Delta^{it}M\Delta^{-it}=M\quad(t\in\mathbb R),\qquad \overline{F_0}=F=S^*.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and write its polar decomposition as $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. The preceding Tomita-operator lemma ensures this closure and polar data are well defined, with $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective. For $x\in\mathcal B(H)$ and dimensionless $t\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sigma_t(x):=\Delta^{it}x\Delta^{-it}.$$
Set $\omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$. The powers $\Delta^{it}$ are the bounded unitary imaginary powers from the unbounded Borel functional calculus. At this definition stage $\sigma_t$ is defined on $\mathcal B(H)$; preservation of $M$ is established by a separate theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector that is cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ on $M\Omega$ and $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and $F=S^*$. Then $S$ is a densely defined closed antilinear involution, its polar decomposition is $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ with $J$ antiunitary and $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective, and
$$J=J^*=J^{-1},\qquad J\Delta J=\Delta^{-1},\qquad J\Delta^{it}J=\Delta^{it}\ (t\in\mathbb R),\qquad F=J\Delta^{-1/2}=\Delta^{1/2}J,\qquad J\Omega=\Omega,\qquad \Delta\Omega=\Omega.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator whose spectral projection valued measure $E$ is supported on $(0,\infty)$. For $\xi\in H$, put $\mu_\xi(B)=\langle E(B)\xi,\xi\rangle$. Define
$$D(A^{1/2})=\left\{\xi\in H:\int_{(0,\infty)}\lambda\,d\mu_\xi(\lambda)<\infty\right\}.$$
For $z\in S=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq1\}$ and $\xi\in D(A^{1/2})$, define $A^{-iz/2}\xi$ by the unbounded Borel functional calculus for the function $\lambda\mapsto \exp(-iz\log(\lambda)/2)$. This vector is defined, strongly continuous in $z$ on $S$, and satisfies
$$\|A^{-iz/2}\xi\|^2\leq\|\xi\|^2+\|A^{1/2}\xi\|^2.$$
The map $z\mapsto A^{-iz/2}\xi$ is norm-holomorphic on the open strip $S^\circ$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von
Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space $H$, and define
$$M_\perp:=\{T\in\mathcal S_1(H):\operatorname{Tr}(Tx)=0 \text{ for every }x\in M\}.$$
Equip the coset space $Q:=\mathcal S_1(H)/M_\perp$ with the quotient norm.
Then the trace pairing
$$\Psi:M\to Q^*,\qquad (\Psi(x))([T])=\operatorname{Tr}(Tx),$$
is a well-defined isometric bijection, and $Q$ is a Banach space. Thus $Q$ is
an isometric predual of $M$, and its dual unit ball is weak-star compact.
Every vector functional $x\mapsto\langle x\xi,\xi\rangle$ and every positive
functional in $Q$ preserves suprema of bounded increasing positive nets in
$M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, and let
$\mathcal S_1(H)$ be its trace-class operators with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
and trace $\operatorname{Tr}$. Finite-rank operators are dense in
$(\mathcal S_1(H),\|\cdot\|_1)$. For every bounded linear functional
$\Phi:\mathcal S_1(H)\to\mathbb C$, there is a unique $X\in\mathcal B(H)$ such
that
$$\Phi(T)=\operatorname{Tr}(TX)\qquad(T\in\mathcal S_1(H)),$$
and the correspondence is isometric:
$\|\Phi\|=\|X\|$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M\ne\{0\}$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space. Use the predual $M_*=Q$ of [[lem-qsmx-von-neumann-predual]]; its elements are the normal linear functionals, and the induced topology $\sigma(M,Q)$ is the ultraweak topology. A **normal state** on $M$ is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:M\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(I)=1$, $\omega(a)\geq0$ for every positive $a\in M$, and
$$\omega\!\left(\sup_i a_i\right)=\sup_i\omega(a_i)$$
for every increasing net $(a_i)$ of positive elements with $0\leq a_i\leq C I$ for a common finite $C$ and supremum taken in $M$.
An automorphism of $M$ is **normal** when it preserves the suprema of all such bounded increasing positive nets.
A **point-ultraweakly continuous one-parameter automorphism group** is a family $(\alpha_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ of bijective unital complex-linear maps $M\to M$ preserving multiplication and adjoints, with $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_M$, $\alpha_s\alpha_t=\alpha_{s+t}$, and $t\mapsto\varphi(\alpha_t(x))$ continuous for every $x\in M$ and every normal linear functional $\varphi\in Q$.
For dimensionless $t$ and dimensionless $\beta>0$, the normal state $\omega$ satisfies the **upper-strip $(\alpha,\beta)$ KMS condition** when, for every $A,B\in M$, there is a bounded scalar function $F_{A,B}$ on $S_\beta=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq\beta\}$ that is continuous on $S_\beta$, holomorphic in its interior, and satisfies
$$F_{A,B}(t)=\omega(A\alpha_t(B)),\qquad F_{A,B}(t+i\beta)=\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)\quad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be a positive self-adjoint injective operator with spectral projection valued measure $E$ supported on $(0,\infty)$. For $t\in\mathbb R$, the unbounded Borel functional calculus defines $A^{it}$ as a unitary on all of $H$. For every $\xi\in H$, the map $t\mapsto A^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $\sigma_t(M)=M$. Each $\sigma_t$ is conjugation by the unitary $\Delta^{it}$, so it is complex-linear, multiplicative, adjoint-preserving and bijective, with inverse $\sigma_{-t}$. The spectral calculus gives $\Delta^{i(s+t)}=\Delta^{is}\Delta^{it}$, hence $\sigma_s\sigma_t=\sigma_{s+t}$ and $\sigma_0=I$. To check normality, let $0\leq a_i\uparrow a$ be a bounded increasing net in $M$. Unitary conjugation is an order isomorphism of $\mathcal B(H)$: if $b$ bounds every $\Delta^{it}a_i\Delta^{-it}$, then $\Delta^{-it}b\Delta^{it}$ bounds every $a_i$, so $a\leq\Delta^{-it}b\Delta^{it}$ and $\Delta^{it}a\Delta^{-it}\leq b$. Thus $\Delta^{it}a_i\Delta^{-it}\uparrow\Delta^{it}a\Delta^{-it}$ in $\mathcal B(H)$. By [F2] the limit is in $M$, hence is also the supremum in $M$. By the definition in [F7], each restriction is a normal $*$-automorphism.

For $A,B\in M$, both $A^*\Omega$ and $B\Omega$ lie in $D(\Delta^{1/2})$, because $Sx\Omega=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$ and $\|Sx\Omega\|=\|\Delta^{1/2}x\Omega\|$. Define $$F_{A,B}(z)=\bigl(\Delta^{i\overline z/2}A^*\Omega\,\big|\,\Delta^{-iz/2}B\Omega\bigr),$$ where $(u|v)=\langle v,u\rangle$ is linear in its second argument. By [F3], both vectors $A^*\Omega$ and $B\Omega$ belong to $D(\Delta^{1/2})$; [F4] then makes each vector factor bounded and continuous on the closed strip. The first is anti-holomorphic as a vector-valued function of $z$ and enters the first, conjugate-linear slot, while the second is holomorphic in the second slot. Hence $F_{A,B}$ is bounded and continuous on the strip and holomorphic inside.

By [F8], $t\mapsto\Delta^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous for every $\xi\in H$. For fixed $x\in M$ and $\xi,\eta\in H$, the coefficient $\langle\sigma_t(x)\xi,\eta\rangle$ is therefore continuous. If $T$ is finite rank, $\operatorname{Tr}(T\sigma_t(x))$ is a finite sum of such continuous coefficients. For arbitrary trace-class $T$, choose finite-rank $T_n\to T$ in trace norm by [F6]; uniformly in $t$, $|\operatorname{Tr}((T-T_n)\sigma_t(x))|\leq\|T-T_n\|_1\|x\|$. Thus every element of the predual $Q$ evaluates continuously on $\sigma_t(x)$, which is point-ultraweak continuity.

Since $\Delta^{it}\Omega=\Omega$ and $\Delta^{it}$ is unitary, $$\omega(\sigma_t(x))=\langle\Delta^{it}x\Omega,\Omega\rangle=\langle x\Omega,\Delta^{-it}\Omega\rangle=\omega(x).$$ So $\omega$ is invariant under $\sigma_t$ and under $\alpha_t=\sigma_{-t}$. Also $\omega(I)=\|\Omega\|^2=1$ and $\omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2\geq0$, so $\omega$ is a state; because $\Omega$ is separating for $M$, this same identity shows that $\omega$ is faithful. By [F5], $\omega$ is a normal vector functional on $M$. Hence it is a faithful normal state as asserted.

For real $t$, unitarity of $\Delta^{it/2}$ and the identity $\Delta^{-it}B\Omega=\sigma_{-t}(B)\Omega$ give $$F_{A,B}(t)=(A^*\Omega|\Delta^{-it}B\Omega)=(\Omega|A\Delta^{-it}B\Omega)=\omega(A\alpha_t(B)).$$ This is the lower boundary in [F7].

At $z=t+i$, $\Delta^{i\overline z/2}A^*\Omega=\Delta^{it/2}J A\Omega$ and $\Delta^{-iz/2}B\Omega=\Delta^{-it/2}J B^*\Omega$, because $Sx\Omega=x^*\Omega$ and $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. By [F2], $J$ commutes with $\Delta^{it/2}$; antiunitarity gives $(Ju|Jv)=(v|u)$. Therefore $$F_{A,B}(t+i)=(\Delta^{-it/2}B^*\Omega|\Delta^{it/2}A\Omega)=(B^*\Omega|\Delta^{it}A\Omega)=\omega(B\sigma_t(A)).$$ Invariance from step 2.2 changes the last expression to $\omega(\sigma_{-t}(B)A)=\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)$, the upper boundary in [F7].

Steps 2.2–3.1 provide the bounded continuous strip function with both required boundary values for each $A,B\in M$. By [F7], $\omega$ is upper-strip $(\alpha,1)$ KMS. Step 1.1 gives the asserted point-ultraweakly continuous automorphism group, and [F2] gives $JMJ=M'$. No norm-continuity assertion on all of $M$ is made.
